chapter: Broadway, tenors, Billie Holiday and Rhythm Club memories
title: Billie Holiday
summary: Her taste in men and decline.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them
story.community_name: Billie Holiday as the musicians knew her

blocks.x: We've kind of been touching on Billie Holiday off and on. Did you know her very well?
Oh god, yeah. My brother used to go with her, Ted.
That didn't last too long, though.
No, no it didn't last too long. Don't know how long, a few months. Yeah, Billie.
What was she like when you knew her?

Oh just great. But Billie liked the wrong type of man. She liked that sporting life. You know, and she got mixed up in that, and that's what, you know, she liked that sporting life, those hustlers, Come up and talk a lot of jive you know, a lot of hole in your head. She just liked the wrong type of man. I don't imagine Billie would have liked a man that would get up and pull a chair out for her so she could sit down to dinner. She'd probably look at him and call him a square. She'd much rather have the type of man say, All right, Baby, you got paid last night, I need $200 to make a note on my car. That's the type she liked. Too bad.
Kind of like just a very self destructive ...
She liked that sporting life, that's what she liked.
Did you see her much frequently in the '30s?
Oh yeah, she used to come by the Metropole. It was pathetic to see Billie come by the Metropole, lay a couple of dollars on her.
She lived up in the West 70s I guess.

Yeah, yeah, to lay two dollars on Billie, God, I remember Billie when she was making $3,000 a night. Big blue mink coat on, things like that, and then to come by and ask you for a couple of dollars. Looking bad, she looked terrible. Half drunk you know, come by, she used to come by and sit in the Metropole all by herself. People used to say there's Billie Holiday over there. Fella she was going with at the time, Poor John.

Nobody liked him at all. Think there was five people to his funeral. John Levy, he was a sporting man. Poor John. He had a gin mill right there at 118th and 8th Avenue or 19th, somewhere around there. Poor John. She had a nice guy just before she died, think it was too late then, you know, she got all strung out there you know and it was too late to save her. Had that record against her. Everybody was afraid to hire her.
I guess her reputation followed her around after that time.
Too bad. Yeah, Billie Holiday, Lady Day. Yeah, she, beautiful. She used call me Ozy. Well see, on the drums it was 'Cozy.' A C and then a O Z Y. O L E. She

always used to call me Ozy Ole. I said 'how you doing, Billie.' And she used to come in and sit around. I just loved Billie, she was a wonderful girl, boy. Too bad. It was her mind and that's the way her mind ruled her.
I guess she had a whole childhood and everything with all that went down, that can really shake you for life.

It's too bad. Yeah, I knew Billie very well. Knew another little gal, Thelma Carpenter. She's another nice gal, got all strung out out there. Nice looking gal. Nice careers ahead of them. They get all wrapped up in something, I don't know what it is. Their minds get carried away doing something, I don't know what the devil it is, Bill, but they do it. Then after they do it I guess they're very sorry, you know, about it. And the result turns out to be bad.
